name: Haymo Halberstatensis
identity: Haymo of Halberstadt (d. 853), Carolingian bishop; the massive PL 116-118 commentary corpus under his name is now attributed by scholars (Riggenbach 1907) to Haimo of Auxerre (d. c. 865)
evidence: The commentaries (Psalms, Isaiah, Twelve Prophets, Pauline epistles, Apocalypse) remain almost entirely untranslated. Only small pieces exist in English: Haimo of Auxerre's Commentary on Jonah (trans. Deborah Everhart, TEAMS Commentary Series) and excerpts of the Apocalypse commentary discussed in the TEAMS series; no translation of the Apocalypse commentary (PL 117:938-1220) or the large Pauline/prophetic commentaries was found.

name: Gerhohus Reicherspergensis
identity: Gerhoh of Reichersberg (1093-1169), provost of Reichersberg, Gregorian-reform polemicist; PL 193-194 contain his Expositio/Tractatus in Psalmos (1144-1169) and polemical works incl. De investigatione Antichristi
evidence: Two targeted searches found no published English translation of any complete work: the Psalms commentary and De investigatione Antichristi circulate only in Latin editions (Migne, Sackur/Scheibelberger, Forgotten Books reprints); English-language scholarship (e.g., Journal of Medieval History 2023 article on Gerhoch and holy war) works from the Latin.

name: Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?)
identity: Pseudo-Jerome: the spuria collected in PL 30 (Breviarium in Psalmos, pseudo-epistles, etc.), works transmitted under Jerome's name but not authentic
evidence: No English translation of the Breviarium in Psalmos or the PL 30 spurious corpus located; the Breviarium is described as a spurious interpolated compilation with only Latin manuscript/PL access. Jerome's authentic psalm homilies were translated (Ewald, FC 48, 1964) but those are a different work; the pseudo-corpus itself remains untranslated.

name: Guillelmus abbas
identity: William of Saint-Thierry (c. 1085-1148), Benedictine abbot of Saint-Thierry, later Cistercian at Signy; Corpus Corporum files for this idno are PL 180 works (Aenigma fidei, De natura corporis et animae, etc.)
evidence: Identified via Corpus Corporum PL file paths (180_Guillelmus-abbas_Aenigma-fidei.xml, 180_Guillelmus-abbas_De-natura-corporis-et-animae.xml). The bulk of William's writings are in English from Cistercian Publications: The Enigma of Faith (trans. Anderson, CF 9, 1973), The Mirror of Faith (trans. Davis, CF 15, 1979), The Golden Epistle, Exposition on the Song of Songs, and more; Wikipedia states the bulk of his writings are available in English translation.

name: Paterius notarius Gregorii I
identity: Paterius (d. c. 606), notary and disciple of Gregory the Great, later bishop of Brescia; compiled the Liber testimoniorum, an anthology of Gregory's exegesis arranged in biblical order (PL 79)
evidence: No English translation of the Liber testimoniorum found. The only translated piece is the (pseudo-Paterius) Testimonies on the Apocalypse of Gregory the Great (PL 79:1107-22, actually by Alulfus of Tournai), translated by Mark DelCogliano per Gumerlock's survey of patristic Revelation commentaries.

name: Wernerus S. Blasii
identity: Werner, abbot of St. Blasien (attribution debated: Werner II of St. Blasien, d. 1178, or Werner of Ellerbach, d. 1126); Libri deflorationum / Deflorationes sanctorum Patrum, a homiliary-anthology of patristic excerpts (PL 157)
evidence: No English translation located in two searches. The Deflorationes (printed Basel 1494; PL 157:1019ff.) is discussed in German scholarship (Archivalia on the authorship question) and was mined by Honorius Augustodunensis for his Speculum Ecclesiae, but circulates only in Latin.

name: Prudentius Trecensis
identity: Prudentius (Galindo) of Troyes (d. 861), Spanish-born Carolingian bishop; continuator of the Annals of St-Bertin and Augustinian predestinarian polemicist against Eriugena (De praedestinatione contra Joannem Scotum, PL 115)
evidence: His portion of the Annals of St-Bertin is fully translated (Janet L. Nelson, Manchester Medieval Sources, 1991), and his Tractoria was translated by Francis X. Gumerlock (Kerux 25:1, 2010; cf. Genke & Gumerlock, Gottschalk and a Medieval Predestination Controversy). The long De praedestinatione contra Joannem Scotum itself remains untranslated.

name: Wibaldus Corbeiensis
identity: Wibald (1098-1158), abbot of Stavelot-Malmedy and Corvey, advisor to Conrad III and Frederick Barbarossa; his letter-book of c. 450 letters (PL 189) is a capital source for 1125-1155
evidence: No English translation of the letter collection found in two searches. The modern scholarly edition is Martina Hartmann's Das Briefbuch Abt Wibalds von Stablo und Corvey (MGH, German/Latin); the TMR review of Hartmann's Studien confirms scholarship works from the Latin. Only paraphrased excerpts appear in English scholarship.

name: Munio Mindoniensis
identity: Munio Alfonso (d. c. 1136), treasurer of Santiago de Compostela, bishop of Mondoñedo 1112-1136; co-author of the Historia Compostellana (he wrote Book I chs. 4-45), the chronicle of Archbishop Diego Gelmírez
evidence: No English translation of the Historia Compostellana exists; the standard edition is Emma Falque's Latin text (CCCM 70, Brepols) with a Spanish translation, and English-language scholarship (Fletcher's Saint James's Catapult; Kawalek's 2022 Birmingham PhD on the Historia's authors) works from Latin/Spanish.

name: Benedictus diaconus
identity: Benedictus Levita ('Benedict the Deacon' of Mainz), pseudonymous 9th-c. forger (c. 847-850) of a three-book collection of false capitularies, part of the Pseudo-Isidorian forgery complex (PL 97)
evidence: No English translation of the False Capitularies exists; the collection is available in Baluze's Capitularia regum Francorum (1677), Pertz's MGH Leges II, and the ongoing MGH edition project in Latin. Neither search found any English translation project for the collection.

name: Hieronymus Radiolensis
identity: Girolamo da Raggiolo (c. 1435-c. 1500), Vallombrosan monk and hagiographer in the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici; his Miracula S. Iohannis Gualberti (dedicated to Lorenzo) is printed in PL 146:811-960
evidence: Identity established via Italian Wikipedia and Vallombrosan bibliography (Salvestrini). No English translation of the Miracula or of his Liber de Vallumbrosanae religionis beatis found; the works circulate in the PL Latin text and in Italian scholarship only.

name: Auctor incertus (Fulgentius Ruspensis?)
identity: Pseudo-Fulgentius: texts transmitted under the name of Fulgentius of Ruspe (467-533), chiefly the Sermones LXXX (PL 65) and other misattributed pieces from Vandal-era North Africa
evidence: The pseudo-Fulgentius sermon corpus has no published English translation (Bodleian catalogs it only in Latin). One pseudo-Fulgentius text, the Book on the Trinity (a Nicene testimonia collection from Vandal Africa, c. 484), is translated by Robin Whelan in his online Vandal Africa sourcebook; FC translations (Fairbairn, McGregor) cover only authentic Fulgentius.

name: Willelmus Calculus
identity: William of Jumièges ('Calculus', c. 1000-after 1070), Norman monk-historian; author of the Gesta Normannorum Ducum (PL 149), the earliest prose account of the Norman Conquest
evidence: Fully translated: Elisabeth M. C. van Houts, The Gesta Normannorum Ducum of William of Jumièges, Orderic Vitalis, and Robert of Torigni, 2 vols., Oxford Medieval Texts (Clarendon, 1992/1995), a dual Latin-English edition based on all 47 manuscripts and including William's full original text.

name: Stephanus III Cisterciensis
identity: Stephen Harding (c. 1060-1134), English-born third abbot of Cîteaux and co-founder of the Cistercian Order; PL 166 material centers on the early Cistercian foundation documents (Carta Caritatis, Exordium) and letters
evidence: The key texts associated with him are translated: Chrysogonus Waddell, Narrative and Legislative Texts from Early Cîteaux (Studia et Documenta 9, 1999) is a dual Latin-English edition of the Exordium Parvum, Carta Caritatis (prior and posterior), and related legislation; these are the standard English versions. Minor letters/monitum may remain untranslated.

name: Berengosus Trevirensis
identity: Berengosus, abbot of St. Maximin at Trier (d. c. 1125); author of De laude et inventione sanctae crucis, a devotional treatise on the True Cross (PL 160)
evidence: Two searches (author + work title; abbey context) surfaced no English translation and almost no English-language discussion; the treatise appears only in the PL Latin text. St. Maximin's Abbey context confirmed but no translation activity found.

name: Nicolaus Claraevallensis
identity: Nicholas of Clairvaux / Nicholas of Montiéramey (d. 1176/78), secretary of Bernard of Clairvaux and skilled imitator of his style; PL corpus comprises his letters and sermons
evidence: His letter collections are fully translated with facing English text: Lena Wahlgren-Smith (ed./trans.), The Letter Collections of Nicholas of Clairvaux, Oxford Medieval Texts (OUP, 2018). His sermons remain untranslated as a corpus, though individual sermons that passed under Bernard's name appear in Cistercian Fathers volumes (e.g., Various Sermons, CF 84, includes Div 19 by Nicholas).

name: Heregerius Lobiensis
identity: Heriger of Lobbes (c. 942-1007), abbot of Lobbes from 990, historian, hagiographer and computist; works include Gesta episcoporum Tungrensium/Leodiensium, vitae of Ursmar, Remaclus, Landoald, and a eucharistic treatise (PL 139)
evidence: No English translation of any of his works located in two searches; the Gesta and the vitae (incl. the metrical Vita Ursmari) exist in Latin editions (Chapeauville, MGH/Koepke) and are studied in Dutch/French/German scholarship (e.g., Verbist).

name: Heraclides Alexandrinus
identity: 'Heraclides of Alexandria' is the fictive author of the Paradisus Heraclidis (PL 74), the medieval Latin recension of Palladius of Galatia's Lausiac History (c. 419-420) misattributed to Heraclides
evidence: The underlying work is fully available in English via translations of Palladius' Greek: W.K. Lowther Clarke (1918, online at tertullian.org) and Robert T. Meyer, Palladius: The Lausiac History (ACW 34, 1965). The Latin Paradisus recension itself has not been separately translated, but its content is entirely covered by these versions.

name: Lucius II
identity: Pope Lucius II (Gherardo Caccianemici dal Orso, d. 15 Feb 1145), pope 1144-1145 during the Roman Commune crisis; PL 179 preserves his letters and privileges
evidence: No collected translation of his letters exists. Isolated letters are translated in the Columbia Epistolae project (e.g., a 1142 letter as cardinal/chancellor, Epistolae letter 196, citing PL 179 ep. 145); otherwise the corpus is untranslated and English treatment is biographical only.

name: Franco Affligemensis
identity: Franco of Afflighem (d. 1135), monk then abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Affligem (Brabant); author of De gratia Dei in twelve books (PL 166:717-808)
evidence: No English translation located in two searches. The Bodleian medieval manuscripts catalog lists De gratia Dei only in Latin; no translation appears in Benedictine or academic series.

name: Auctor incertus (Hildefonsus Toletanus?)
identity: Pseudo-Ildefonsus: sermons and dubia transmitted under the name of Ildefonsus of Toledo (c. 607-667) in PL 96, largely Marian sermons from the Homiliary of Toledo that Migne himself flagged as doubtful
evidence: The pseudo-Ildefonsus sermons have no English translation (studied in Spanish scholarship on Visigothic homiletics and in work on Marian commemoration in Visigothic Iberia). The genuine Ildefonsian De virginitate perpetua Sanctae Mariae was translated by Malcolm Drew Donalson (Edwin Mellen Press, 2011), which covers the authentic core if any is included in this corpus.

name: Petrus Amelius
identity: Pierre Ameil (Petrus Amelii, d. 1401), Augustinian, patriarch of Grado, papal master of ceremonies during the Great Western Schism; author of the papal ceremonial printed as 'Ordo Romanus XV' in PL 78
evidence: No English translation exists. The modern edition is Marc Dykmans, Le Ceremonial papal IV: Le retour a Rome ou le ceremonial du patriarche Pierre Ameil (Brussels-Rome, 1985), in Latin with French apparatus; English scholarship (Joelle Rollo-Koster on Ameil and papal funerals) quotes and paraphrases but does not translate the ordo.

name: Arnoldus Emmerammensis
identity: Arnold of Saint Emmeram (c. 1000-c. 1050), Benedictine prior, scholar and composer at St. Emmeram, Regensburg; author of De miraculis et memoria cultorum Sancti Emmerami and a dialogue on the saint (PL 141)
evidence: No English translation of De miraculis located in two searches; the text is cited from Latin manuscripts (Munich BSB Clm 14870) and PL in English scholarship, with no translation in any series.

name: Hincmarus Laudunensis
identity: Hincmar of Laon (c. 838-879), Carolingian bishop of Laon, nephew and adversary of Hincmar of Reims; deposed at the Synod of Douzy (871) and blinded; PL 124 preserves his Rotula prolixa and dispute documents
evidence: No English translations of Hincmar of Laon's own writings found. The Collaborative Hincmar Project blog notes that relatively few works of even Hincmar of Reims are translated; the Laon dossier exists in Schieffer's MGH edition (Die Streitschriften Hinkmars von Reims und Hinkmars von Laon) and is treated in English only via studies (McKeon; Stone/West).

name: Mamertus Claudianus
identity: Claudianus Mamertus (d. c. 473), Gallo-Roman priest of Vienne, brother of Bishop Mamertus; author of De statu animae (c. 470, PL 53), defending the soul's incorporeality against Faustus of Riez; dedicated to Sidonius Apollinaris
evidence: No English translation of De statu animae exists; a survey source states this explicitly ('no English translation of Mamertus' wonderfully written and highly erudite book exists'). There is a Spanish translation (Manuel Manas Nunez, UPSA) and an unpublished Boston College dissertation (S. R. Cain 2016) studying the work; the standard edition remains Engelbrecht's CSEL (1885).

name: Bruno Magdeburgensis
identity: Bruno of Merseburg / Bruno the Saxon (fl. 1082), cleric serving the archbishop of Magdeburg and then the bishop of Merseburg; author of Saxonicum bellum / Historia de bello Saxonico on the Saxon revolts against Henry IV
evidence: First complete English translation published: Bruno of Merseburg, The Saxon War, trans. Bernard S. Bachrach and David S. Bachrach (Catholic University of America Press, 2022). Earlier partial translations (Tribur/Oppenheim 1076, Canossa 1077 chapters) circulated via academia.edu and Leeds extracts.

name: Falco Beneventanus
identity: Falco of Benevento (c. 1070-1144), Lombard notary and judge of the papal palace in Benevento; author of the Chronicon Beneventanum covering 1102-1144, the only southern-Italian communal-style chronicle of its era
evidence: Fully translated: 'The Chronicle of Falco of Benevento', trans. G. A. Loud, in Roger II and the Creation of the Kingdom of Sicily (Manchester Medieval Sources, Manchester University Press, 2012), pp. 130-249, fully annotated. Italian dual edition also exists (D'Angelo, Per Verba/Sismel).

name: Robertus S. Remigii
identity: Robert the Monk / Robert of Reims (c. 1055-1122), sometime abbot of Saint-Remi, prior of Senuc; author of the Historia Iherosolimitana (c. 1107-1120, PL 155), the most popular Latin chronicle of the First Crusade, incl. an eyewitness account of Clermont 1095
evidence: Fully translated: Carol Sweetenham, Robert the Monk's History of the First Crusade: Historia Iherosolimitana (Crusade Texts in Translation 11, Ashgate, 2005) - the complete nine books from Clermont to Ascalon.

name: Coelestinus I
identity: Pope Celestine I (pope 422-432); his letters (PL 50) concern the Nestorian controversy, Pelagianism, Gaul, Illyricum, and the mission of Palladius to Ireland; he commissioned Cyril to act against Nestorius
evidence: His Nestorian-controversy correspondence is translated in English within the Council of Ephesus dossier (letter to the Synod of Ephesus and related letters at papalencyclicals.net and in NPNF series 2 vol. 14 / orthodoxchurchfathers.com); four letters of March 431 survive in Greek retranslation and are treated in English sources. The full PL 50 letter corpus has no dedicated collected translation.

name: Reginhardus Sigebergensis
identity: Reginhard (d. 1105), second abbot of Michaelsberg Abbey, Siegburg (1076-1105), man of learning who commissioned/inspired the Vita Annonis of Anno II of Cologne (and possibly the Annolied); small Latin corpus under his name in PL
evidence: No English translation of anything by or associated with Reginhard found in two searches. Even the Vita Annonis Minor exists only in a Latin-German edition (Mauritius Mittler, 1975); Reginhard's own PL texts attract no English-language attention.

name: Carolus II Calvus
identity: Charles the Bald (823-877), king of West Francia and emperor; PL 124 preserves letters, charters and capitularies issued under his name (products of his chancery and councils)
evidence: Only selected items are translated: the Edict of Pitres (864) exists in a full English translation with commentary (UMN thesis at conservancy.umn.edu) and in excerpt at the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook; other capitularies (Servais 854, Quierzy 877) are translated piecemeal in scholarship/blogs. No collected translation of the corpus.

name: Goscelinus Cantuariensis
identity: Goscelin of Saint-Bertin / of Canterbury (c. 1035-after 1107), Flemish monk-hagiographer in England; author of the Liber confortatorius (for the recluse Eva) and many saints' lives incl. the Vita/Historia of Augustine of Canterbury and the Legend of Edith
evidence: Major works are translated: Monika Otter, Goscelin of St Bertin: The Book of Encouragement and Consolation [Liber Confortatorius] (D.S. Brewer, 2004; pbk 2012, Library of Medieval Women) - verified; and the Legend of Edith in Stephanie Hollis et al., Writing the Wilton Women (Brepols, 2004). His large Canterbury hagiographic dossier (Historia maior/minor of St Augustine, PL 155) remains mostly untranslated.

name: Gerardus presbyter
identity: Most plausibly Gerhard of Augsburg (fl. 982-993), cathedral cleric/provost and collaborator of Bishop Ulrich; author of the Vita sancti Uodalrici (PL 135), the biography that secured the first papal canonization (993)
evidence: No English translation exists. The modern critical edition is Latin-German only: Walter Berschin and Angelika Haese, Gerhard von Augsburg, Vita Sancti Uodalrici (Editiones Heidelbergenses 24, Winter, 2nd ed. 2020), including the 993 canonization bull. English scholarship discusses but does not translate the vita. Identification of this PL idno with Gerhard is probable but not externally certified.
